title: File-based apps
hook: Starting with C# 14 and the .NET 10 SDK you can `dotnet run hello.cs` with no `.csproj`. Directives that start with `#:` are the project file, inlined.

sections.heading: Single-file programs on .NET 10
sections.prose: File-based apps compile and run one `.cs` file. `dotnet run app.cs`, `dotnet app.cs`, or a Unix shebang `#!/usr/bin/env dotnet` all work. Use them for spikes: dump a Redis key, parse a CSV sample, mint a JWT locally. They are not a replacement for a multi-project worker. `dotnet project convert app.cs` emits a real csproj when the file grows. Native AOT publish is on by default for these apps; turn it off with a property directive if you need reflection. Do not nest the file under an existing `.csproj` tree — implicit MSBuild files will fight you.

snippets.label: File-based app with C# 14 hash-colon directives
snippets.explanation: `#:` directives (package, property, sdk, project, include) configure the virtual project. They are not classic `#if` preprocessor symbols.

sections.heading: What belongs in a worker vs a file
sections.prose: An SQS consumer with tests, multiple types, and CI belongs in an SDK project. A one-off “decode this auth token payload” script can stay a file-based app. The language is the same C# 14; only the host project is virtual.

interviewTakeaways: File-based apps are a .NET 10 SDK feature using C# 14 `#:` directives, not a C# 11 language change.
Classic preprocessor (`#if`, `#region`) still exists; `#:` is SDK configuration in source.
Convert to a project when you need multiple compile items, shared props, or a stable CI graph.
commonPitfalls: Dating file-based apps to C# 11 because top-level statements arrived earlier — those are independent.
Putting `utility.cs` inside a csproj directory and wondering why restore picks the project instead of the file.
Relying on default PublishAot and then missing a reflection-based serializer.

jsTsCorrelations.note: `node file.mjs` runs source. `dotnet run file.cs` still compiles (virtual project) then runs. Shebang exists in both ecosystems.
